title: Reading and Judging Evidence
bigQuestion: How can you tell whether a scientific claim deserves your belief?

story.title: The Map and the Pump Handle
story.kicker: In the summer of 1854 a London doctor drew dots on a street map and found the source of a killer that everyone else blamed on bad air.
paragraphs: At the end of August 1854, cholera exploded in Soho, a crowded neighborhood of London. Cholera kills by violent diarrhea and vomiting that drain the body of water; a healthy adult could sicken at breakfast and be dead by night. Within ten days more than five hundred people in a few streets were dead. Families fled. The accepted explanation, held by most doctors and the government, was miasma: a poisonous vapor rising from filth and sewage and drifting through the air.

John Snow, a physician who lived nearby, did not believe it. He had studied earlier outbreaks and suspected that cholera was swallowed, not inhaled, and that it spread through water fouled by the waste of the sick. But suspecting is not showing. So Snow went door to door with the registrar's list of deaths and marked each one on a map of the streets. The dots piled up around one spot: the public water pump on Broad Street.

A pattern on a map is a correlation, and Snow knew a skeptic would say the pump was simply in the middle of a crowded, dirty district. So he hunted for the cases that did not fit. A brewery a few doors from the pump had lost no workers; the men drank the beer they made and never touched the pump. A workhouse with its own private well, housing hundreds of people, was nearly untouched. And a widow who had moved to Hampstead, miles away, died of cholera after having a bottle of Broad Street water delivered because she liked its taste.

On September 7 Snow presented his evidence to the parish officials. The next day they removed the pump handle. The outbreak was already fading, and Snow himself admitted that the handle probably did not end it. What mattered was the argument: a claim, evidence gathered on foot, reasoning that explained both the pattern and the exceptions, and a prediction that could be checked. A local clergyman, Henry Whitehead, set out to prove Snow wrong, gathered his own data, and ended up finding the first case: a sick baby whose washing water had drained into a cesspool beside the well.

The cholera bacterium itself was not confirmed under the microscope until the 1880s, three decades later. Snow never saw the cause. He found it anyway, because he treated a popular belief as a claim to be tested rather than a fact to be accepted. This chapter is about doing what Snow did: reading evidence honestly, asking what else could explain it, and knowing when a claim has earned belief.
story.think: Snow's map alone could not prove the pump was the cause. Which of his other pieces of evidence do you think did the most to rule out the miasma explanation, and why?

lessons.title: What a Claim Needs
lessons.mainIdea: A scientific claim is an answer to a question that is backed by evidence and linked to that evidence by clear reasoning.
reading: A fish kill at a park pond gets people talking. One neighbor says a factory dumped poison; another says the heat wave did it. Each of these is a *claim*: a statement that answers a question about what happened or why. A claim is not right or wrong just because someone says it with confidence. It becomes worth believing only when it is tied to *evidence*, meaning observations and measurements that anyone could check.

Evidence by itself does not settle anything. A dissolved-oxygen reading of 1.5 milligrams per liter is just a number until someone explains why it matters. That link is the *reasoning*: the scientific principle that connects the evidence to the claim. Warm water holds less oxygen, decaying algae use up what is left, and most fish suffocate below about 2 milligrams per liter. Now the number supports the heat-wave claim, and the poison claim needs its own evidence.

Good scientific claims share one more feature. They are *falsifiable*: there is some observation that would show them to be wrong. 'The fish died because of low oxygen' can be checked against oxygen readings, fish species and the timing of the deaths. 'The fish died because the pond was unlucky' cannot be checked at all. A claim that no possible evidence could ever count against is not a scientific claim, however attractive it sounds.

Throughout this unit you will use this claim, evidence and reasoning pattern to take arguments apart and to build your own. The questions to ask are always the same. What exactly is being claimed? What evidence is offered, and could I look at it myself? What reasoning links the two, and does that reasoning hold up? And what would it take to show the claim is wrong?

words.d: a statement that answers a scientific question about what happens or why it happens
observations, measurements and data that can be checked and that bear on a claim
the scientific principle or logic that explains why the evidence supports the claim
able to be shown wrong by some possible observation or test

look.title: Three Words Over the Door
look.cite: Motto of the Royal Society of London, adopted in the 1660s; Latin for 'take nobody's word for it'
look.prompt: The founders of one of the first scientific societies chose this motto. What habit of mind were they trying to build, and how does it connect to the idea of evidence?

check.q: In the fish-kill example, which of these is the reasoning rather than the claim or the evidence?
choices: Warm water holds less oxygen, and fish suffocate below about 2 milligrams per liter
The fish died because of the heat wave
The oxygen reading was 1.5 milligrams per liter
A neighbor said the factory dumped poison
check.why: Reasoning is the principle that links the measurement to the claim; the oxygen reading is evidence and the heat-wave statement is the claim.

check.q: Why is 'the pond was unlucky' not a scientific claim?
choices: It is too short to be a claim
No possible observation could show it to be wrong
It does not mention a number
Nobody important said it
check.why: A scientific claim must be falsifiable; luck explains everything and therefore can be tested by nothing.

check.q: A student says, 'My claim must be true because I am very sure of it.' What is missing?
choices: A longer explanation of the feeling
A vote from the class
Evidence that others could check, and reasoning that links it to the claim
A famous scientist who agrees
check.why: Confidence is not evidence; a claim earns belief through checkable observations and sound reasoning, not through certainty or authority.

lessons.title: Correlation Is Not Causation
lessons.mainIdea: Two things that rise and fall together may be linked by a hidden third factor, by chance, or by cause running the other way.
reading: In most American cities, ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise and fall together across the year. Nobody believes that ice cream causes drowning. Both rise in summer, when people swim more and eat more cold treats. Summer is a *confounding variable*: a hidden factor that drives both things and creates a *correlation* between them. A correlation means two quantities move together. *Causation* means one actually produces the other.

There are three main ways a correlation can fool you. First, a confounder like the season may cause both. Second, the cause may run backward: hospitals with more patients in intensive care have more deaths, but the care is not killing them; the sickest patients are sent there. Third, with enough pairs of numbers, some will line up by pure chance. If you compare a hundred unrelated things, a few will match closely by accident, and a careless researcher will report those few.

So how did scientists ever conclude that smoking causes cancer, when no one can run an experiment forcing people to smoke? In 1965 the British statistician Austin Bradford Hill laid out a set of questions. Is the association strong? Does more of the cause bring more of the effect? Does the cause come before the effect in time? Does the link show up in many different studies and populations? Is there a known mechanism? No single answer proves causation, but together they build a case that a chance correlation cannot match.

The strongest tool is still the controlled experiment, where you change one factor on purpose and hold the rest steady. When that is impossible or unethical, scientists lean on the Bradford Hill questions, on natural experiments, and on looking hard for confounders. When you read that 'a study links' one thing to another, your first question should be: what else could explain this?

words.d: a pattern in which two quantities tend to rise or fall together
a relationship in which one thing actually produces a change in another
a hidden factor that affects both quantities and creates a misleading correlation between them

look.title: More Firefighters, More Damage
look.text: A city analyst studies a year of fire reports. She finds a strong correlation: the more firefighters sent to a fire, the greater the dollar value of damage. A council member proposes sending fewer firefighters to each fire to reduce damage.
look.prompt: What is the confounding variable here, and what would happen if the council member's plan were adopted?

check.q: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together each summer. What best explains the correlation?
choices: Eating ice cream causes cramps that lead to drowning
News of drownings makes people crave ice cream
It is a coincidence with no explanation
Warm weather increases both swimming and ice cream eating
check.why: Season is a confounding variable that drives both quantities, so they move together without either causing the other.

check.q: Which of these is an example of the cause running backward?
choices: Intensive care units have more deaths because the sickest patients are sent there
Tall people tend to have longer arms
Cities with more cars have more traffic
Plants given more water grow more
check.why: Being near death causes a patient to be in intensive care, not the other way around; that is reverse causation.

check.q: Why did Bradford Hill propose a set of questions instead of a single test for causation?
choices: Because experiments were not yet invented in 1965
Because when experiments are impossible, many kinds of evidence together build a case that chance cannot match
Because correlation always proves causation if the sample is large
Because a single question would be too hard to remember
check.why: When you cannot run a controlled experiment, strength, dose-response, timing, consistency and mechanism together make a causal case that a coincidence could not produce.

lessons.title: Samples, Bias and Controls
lessons.mainIdea: A conclusion is only as good as the sample it rests on, and a fair sample needs a comparison group chosen the same way.
reading: In 1936 the magazine Literary Digest mailed about ten million ballots asking Americans how they would vote for president. More than two million came back, an enormous *sample*, and the magazine confidently predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt. Roosevelt won in one of the biggest landslides in history. The mailing list had been built from telephone directories and car registrations, and in the middle of the Depression the people who owned phones and cars were richer than average and leaned against Roosevelt. A young pollster named George Gallup, using a far smaller but carefully chosen sample, got it right.

The lesson is that size does not cure *bias*. Bias is any systematic way that a sample differs from the population it is supposed to represent. Surveying only people who answer the phone, only patients who came back to the clinic, or only the mice that survived the first week all build bias into the result. The cure is random selection, where every member of the population has an equal chance of being picked, so that the sample's differences from the population are only due to chance, and chance shrinks as the sample grows.

A second kind of fairness is the *control group*. In 1747 the ship's surgeon James Lind took twelve sailors sick with scurvy, kept them on the same diet in the same quarters, and gave each pair a different treatment. The pair who got oranges and lemons recovered within days; the others did not. Without the comparison, a recovery proves nothing, because people often recover on their own. Modern trials go further: patients are assigned to groups at random, the control group gets a *placebo* that looks identical, and neither patients nor doctors know who got which until the end.

When you read a study, ask three questions. How were the subjects chosen, and who was left out? Was there a control group, and was it treated exactly the same except for the one thing being tested? And how large was the sample, remembering that a small random sample beats a huge biased one every time?

words.d: the part of a population that is actually measured or surveyed
a systematic difference between a sample and the population it is meant to represent
a comparison group treated the same as the test group except for the one factor being studied
a fake treatment that looks like the real one, used so that the control group's experience matches the test group's

look.title: How Much a Random Sample Can Miss
look.cite: Standard rule of thumb for a random sample: about 1 divided by the square root of the sample size, rounded
look.prompt: Quadrupling the sample only halves the uncertainty. Why might a pollster stop at a few thousand people rather than surveying millions?

check.q: Why did the Literary Digest poll fail despite more than two million responses?
choices: Two million is too small a sample
The ballots were counted incorrectly
The people surveyed were richer than average and did not represent all voters
Roosevelt changed his mind after the poll
check.why: The sample was biased toward phone and car owners, and no amount of size fixes a systematic bias.

check.q: What made Lind's scurvy test convincing rather than a lucky story?
choices: He used the largest ship in the navy
He gave everyone oranges and lemons
He wrote up the result the same day
He kept the sailors' conditions the same and compared different treatments side by side
check.why: Comparison groups under matched conditions show that the recovery came from the treatment, not from time or chance.

check.q: Why do modern drug trials give the control group a placebo?
choices: So the control group's experience matches the test group's in everything but the drug
To save money on the real drug
Because placebos cure most diseases
So that the control group knows it is the control group
check.why: Expecting a treatment can change how people feel and report; a matching placebo keeps expectations equal so only the drug differs.

lessons.title: Reading a Graph Honestly
lessons.mainIdea: A graph can tell the truth or bend it depending on its axes, its scale and the window of data it chooses to show.
reading: The same data can be drawn to look like a crisis or like nothing at all. Suppose a city's water use fell from 100 million gallons a day to 97 million over a decade. Plotted on an *axis* that runs from 0 to 100, the line is nearly flat. Plotted on an axis that runs from 96 to 100, the same line plunges toward the floor. Neither graph lies about the numbers, but one of them lies about their importance. Before you read the line, read the axes: where they start, what units they use and whether the *scale* is evenly spaced.

The second trick is the window. A stock that has fallen for five years can look like a winner if the chart shows only the last three months. Choosing the start and end points that make your case is called *cherry-picking*, and it is the most common way honest-looking graphs mislead. Ask what happened just before the graph begins and whether a longer view would change the story. A real *trend* holds up when you widen the window.

Watch also for two lines on two different vertical axes, which can be stretched to make anything appear to match anything; for bars whose width or picture size grows along with their height, so the eye sees a bigger change than the numbers show; and for lines with no error bars at all, which hide how uncertain each point is. A logarithmic scale, where each step up multiplies by ten, is not a trick, but it does make explosive growth look like a gentle slope, so check the labels.

None of this means graphs are untrustworthy. A well-made graph shows in one glance what would take a page of numbers to say. The habit to build is simply to read a graph the way you read a contract: the labels, the units, the range, the source and the sample size first, and the dramatic line last.

words.d: one of the two number lines a graph is drawn on, showing the range and units of a variable
how much each step along an axis represents, which can be even, stretched or logarithmic
choosing only the data points or time window that support your case
the overall direction of change in data over time, seen when the window is wide enough

look.title: Two Graphs, One Data Set
look.text: A company's ad shows a bar chart titled 'Our battery lasts longer.' Two bars: theirs reaches nearly the top of the chart, the rival's is a stub. The vertical axis, in small print, runs from 9.8 hours to 10.2 hours. The bars represent 10.1 hours and 9.9 hours.
look.prompt: Redraw the chart in your mind with an axis starting at zero. How big is the difference, and what would you need to know about the sample to decide whether even that difference is real?

check.q: A graph's vertical axis starts at 96 instead of 0. What effect does this have?
choices: It changes the actual numbers
It makes small changes look large
It makes the graph more accurate
It removes the need for units
check.why: Truncating the axis stretches a small range across the whole height of the graph, exaggerating small differences.

check.q: What is the best way to check whether a rising line is a real trend or a cherry-picked window?
choices: Look for a thicker line
Trust the graph if it has a title
Widen the time window and see whether the pattern holds
Check that the line is red
check.why: A genuine trend survives a longer view; a cherry-picked window falls apart when you look before the chosen start date.

check.q: On a logarithmic vertical axis, what does each equal step upward represent?
choices: Adding one unit
Adding ten units
Doubling the value
Multiplying the value by ten
check.why: On a log scale each equal step multiplies by a fixed factor, usually ten, so rapid growth looks like a gentle slope.

lessons.title: Error and Uncertainty
lessons.mainIdea: Every measurement carries uncertainty, and honest science reports how large that uncertainty is instead of hiding it.
reading: Measure a table with a meter stick and you might get 152.3 centimeters. Measure again and get 152.1. Neither is a mistake. In science the word error does not mean a blunder; it means the unavoidable gap between a measurement and the true value. Every instrument has a finest mark, every hand wobbles, every room changes temperature. The size of that gap is the *uncertainty*, and a measurement reported without it is only half reported.

Errors come in two kinds. *Random error* scatters readings above and below the true value with no pattern, like the wobble of a hand-held ruler. Repeating the measurement and averaging shrinks random error, because the highs and lows cancel. *Systematic error* pushes every reading the same way, like a scale that reads 2 grams heavy with nothing on it. Averaging does nothing for it; you find it only by checking the instrument against a known standard. A tight cluster of readings tells you the *precision* is high; it does not tell you they are *accurate*.

The measured speed of light shows how uncertainty gets smaller over time. Hippolyte Fizeau in 1849 used a spinning toothed wheel and got a value about 5 percent too high. Albert Michelson, using rotating mirrors and a long baseline, narrowed the range to a few kilometers per second by the 1920s. Each later scientist did not simply announce a number; they announced a number with a plus-or-minus, and the next experiment had to land inside or outside that range.

When you read a result, look for the plus-or-minus, the error bars on a graph or the words 'confidence interval.' Two measurements that differ by less than their uncertainties agree; nothing has been discovered. A difference that is many times larger than the uncertainty is a real signal. Learning to tell those apart is most of what it means to read data.

words.d: the range within which the true value of a measurement probably lies, often written as plus-or-minus
unpredictable scatter in repeated measurements that averaging can reduce
a consistent shift in every measurement in the same direction, caused by the instrument or method
how closely repeated measurements agree with one another
how close a measurement is to the true value

look.title: Closing In on the Speed of Light
look.cite: Historic measurements as commonly reported, rounded; since 1983 the value is fixed by definition of the meter
look.prompt: Michelson's 1879 value carried an uncertainty of about plus or minus 50 km/s. Does the modern value fall inside his range? What does that tell you about his work?

check.q: A kitchen scale reads 2 grams with nothing on it, so every reading is 2 grams too high. What kind of error is this?
choices: Systematic error
Random error
Rounding error
Sampling error
check.why: The error pushes every reading the same direction by the same amount, which is the definition of systematic error.

check.q: Which technique reduces random error but not systematic error?
choices: Buying a more expensive instrument
Repeating the measurement and averaging
Rounding to fewer digits
Measuring only once, very carefully
check.why: Averaging cancels random highs and lows, but a consistent shift is present in every reading and survives the average.

check.q: Five readings of a length cluster tightly around 30.2 cm, but the true length is 31.0 cm. How should the readings be described?
choices: Accurate but not precise
Both accurate and precise
Precise but not accurate
Neither precise nor accurate
check.why: Precision is how well readings agree with each other; accuracy is closeness to the true value. Tight agreement around the wrong value is precise but inaccurate.

lessons.title: Significant Figures and False Precision
lessons.mainIdea: The digits you report should match what your instrument can actually tell you; extra digits claim a certainty you do not have.
reading: A ruler marked in millimeters lets you read a pencil as 14.7 centimeters, with the last digit an honest estimate between marks. Writing 14.7000 centimeters would claim you know the length to a ten-thousandth of a centimeter, which the ruler cannot support. The digits that carry real information are the *significant figures*. In 14.7 there are three. The rule of the game is simple: report every digit you can defend and not one more.

Calculators are the main source of trouble. Divide a 14.7 centimeter pencil into 3 equal pieces and the screen says 4.9 centimeters; divide 14.7 by 7 and it shows 2.1, but the screen may first show 2.1000000. Those extra zeros mean nothing. A result cannot be more precise than the least precise measurement that went into it. When multiplying or dividing, keep the same number of significant figures as the measurement with the fewest. When adding or subtracting, keep the same number of decimal places as the roughest measurement. Counting numbers, like 3 pieces, are exact and do not limit anything.

The same idea guards you against *false precision* outside the lab. A headline that says the average adult walks 3,812 steps a day sounds exact, but a survey of a few hundred people with step counters of unknown quality cannot pin the number to the last step. A report that a hurricane has a 47.3 percent chance of landfall is claiming more than any forecast model can deliver. When a number carries more digits than its source could possibly justify, it is a sign that someone wants it to sound more certain than it is.

*Rounding* is therefore not laziness; it is honesty. Say about 3,800 steps, roughly a 50 percent chance, 4.9 centimeters. Keep the extra digits in your calculator during the work so rounding errors do not pile up, and round once at the end to the precision your data can actually support.

words.d: the digits in a measurement that carry real information, from the first nonzero digit to the estimated last digit
reporting more digits than the measurement or method can justify
trimming a number to the digits that the underlying data can support

look.title: The Calculator's Nine Digits
look.text: A student measures a block on a balance that reads to the nearest 0.1 gram: 24.6 grams. She measures its sides with a ruler: 2.0 cm, 3.1 cm and 4.2 cm. Her calculator gives a volume of 26.04 cubic centimeters and a density of 0.944700461 grams per cubic centimeter. She writes all nine digits in her report.
look.prompt: Which measurement limits her precision, and how many significant figures should the density have? What would a reader wrongly conclude from nine digits?

check.q: A length of 14.7 cm is divided by an exact count of 3. How should the result be reported?
choices: 5 cm
4.9 cm
check.why: The count of 3 is exact, so the measurement 14.7 with three significant figures sets the limit, and 4.9 keeps that precision without adding false digits.

check.q: Why is a headline claiming '3,812 steps a day' an example of false precision?
choices: The survey and the step counters could not justify accuracy to the single step
Step counts are always rounded to thousands by law
Four-digit numbers cannot be significant
People do not walk in steps
check.why: The number carries more digits than the sample size and instruments could support, so it sounds more certain than it is.

check.q: When should you round during a multi-step calculation?
choices: After every step, to keep it simple
Once, at the end, to the precision the data supports
Never; report every calculator digit
Only when the teacher asks
check.why: Rounding at every step lets small errors pile up; keeping extra digits during work and rounding once at the end is both accurate and honest.

lessons.title: Peer Review and Replication
lessons.mainIdea: Science trusts a result not because an expert approved it but because others can repeat it and get the same answer.
reading: Before a scientific paper appears in a journal, editors send it to other scientists in the field for *peer review*. The reviewers look for weak methods, missing controls, overreaching conclusions and math errors, and they can demand changes or recommend rejection. Peer review catches a great deal, but it is not proof. Reviewers rarely see the raw data, cannot repeat the experiment, and are volunteers working for free. A peer-reviewed paper is a serious claim worth taking seriously, not a settled fact.

The deeper test is *replication*: can a different lab, following the published methods, get the same result? In March 1989 two chemists at the University of Utah announced at a press conference that they had produced nuclear fusion in a jar of water at room temperature. Labs around the world rushed to repeat it. Within months most had failed, the few early successes evaporated, and the claim collapsed. That is the system working. In 2015 a team of psychologists tried to repeat 100 published experiments and found that fewer than half held up, which has pushed many fields to raise their standards.

When a published paper turns out to be wrong through fraud or serious error, the journal issues a *retraction*, formally withdrawing it from the record. Retractions are rare and painful, but a field without them would be a field that never admits mistakes. Many scientists now also post *preprints*, drafts shared online before review, so that colleagues can criticize the work early. A preprint has not passed review at all, and news stories built on preprints deserve extra caution.

The lesson for a reader is that no single study is the final word. Ask whether the result has been repeated by independent groups, whether the raw data and methods are available, and whether the finding fits with the rest of what is known. A surprising result from one lab is a lead. A result that many labs have reproduced is knowledge.

words.d: the checking of a scientific paper by other experts before a journal publishes it
repeating a study independently to see whether the same result appears
the formal withdrawal of a published paper because of serious error or misconduct
a draft scientific paper posted publicly before it has been peer reviewed

look.title: The Easiest Person to Fool
look.text: Feynman told graduating students that the first rule of doing science honestly is that you must not fool yourself, and that you are the easiest person for you to fool. Once you have managed that, he said, it becomes easy not to fool other scientists, because you must simply report everything that could make your result wrong, not only what supports it.
look.cite: Richard Feynman, commencement address at the California Institute of Technology, 1974 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why does Feynman say the hardest person to be honest with is yourself? How do peer review and replication help with a problem that lives inside each scientist?

check.q: What does passing peer review guarantee about a paper?
choices: That the raw data have been checked line by line
That the experiment has been repeated by another lab
That experts judged its methods and conclusions reasonable, though it may still be wrong
That it is settled scientific fact
check.why: Reviewers judge the paper's methods and logic, but they usually cannot see the raw data or repeat the work, so peer review is a filter, not proof.

check.q: What happened to the 1989 claim of room-temperature fusion?
choices: It was confirmed and won a Nobel Prize
It was ignored because nobody tried to repeat it
It is still being tested today with no result
Labs worldwide failed to replicate it, and the claim collapsed within months
check.why: Replication is the real test; when independent labs could not reproduce the result, the scientific community set it aside.

check.q: A news story reports an exciting result from a preprint. Why should a reader be extra cautious?
choices: A preprint has not yet been checked by peer reviewers or repeated by anyone
Preprints are always written by students
Preprints are printed on cheap paper
News stories never report on real science
check.why: A preprint is a draft that has skipped even the first filter of peer review, so its claims are the least tested kind of published science.

lessons.title: Judging a Science News Story
lessons.mainIdea: A science headline is a claim about a claim; check who did the study, on whom, how big the effect really is and who paid for it.
reading: Headlines compress. A study that found a small effect in 40 mice over eight weeks becomes 'Coffee Cures Memory Loss' by the time it reaches your feed. The first questions to ask of any science story are the ones a scientist would ask of the paper behind it. Who did the study, and was it published in a peer-reviewed journal? What was studied, humans or animals or cells in a dish? How many subjects, and for how long? Was there a control group? Most stories that fall apart fall apart here.

The second trap is how risk is described. In 2015 a World Health Organization agency reported that eating about 50 grams of processed meat a day raised the *relative risk* of colorectal cancer by about 18 percent. Headlines compared bacon to cigarettes. But the lifetime *absolute risk* of colorectal cancer is around 5 or 6 percent, so an 18 percent increase moves it by about one percentage point. Both numbers are true. Only the absolute number tells you how much it matters to you, and stories almost always give you the relative one because it is bigger.

Third, follow the money and the megaphone. A university *press release* is written to attract attention, and a study of the topic found that exaggeration in news stories often begins in the release itself. A *conflict of interest*, such as a study of a sweetener funded by a sweetener company, does not prove the result is wrong, but it raises the bar for how carefully you should check it. Good journals require authors to declare funding; good stories mention it.

Finally, one study is one study. Science moves by the weight of many results, and a single paper that overturns decades of evidence is far more likely to be wrong than to be a revolution. The most reliable science stories are the least exciting ones: they report a body of work, quote scientists who were not involved, give absolute numbers and say plainly what is still unknown.

words.d: how much a factor multiplies the chance of an outcome compared with people without that factor
the actual chance of an outcome, such as 5 in 100, before or after a factor is added
a promotional summary of a study written by an institution to attract news coverage
a situation in which a researcher or funder stands to gain from a particular result

look.title: Chocolate Makes You Smarter
look.text: A headline reads: 'Study: Eating chocolate daily boosts brain power.' The story, read to the end, says the study followed 20 adults for two weeks, measured their scores on one puzzle test, found a small improvement with no control group, and was funded by a chocolate maker. The lead researcher is quoted saying more work is needed.
look.prompt: List every weakness in this study that the headline hides. What kind of study would actually be needed to support the headline's claim?

check.q: A story says a food raises cancer risk by 18 percent. What number do you need to know how much that matters?
choices: The price of the food
The absolute risk before and after eating the food
The number of headlines about it
The relative risk of a different disease
check.why: Relative risk multiplies a baseline; only the absolute risk tells you the actual change in your chances, which was about one percentage point in the processed meat case.

check.q: Why is a study funded by the maker of the product being tested a concern?
choices: Because company scientists are never trained
Because funded studies are always false
Because the funder gains from one outcome, so the result needs closer checking
Because journals refuse to publish such studies
check.why: A conflict of interest does not prove a result wrong, but it raises the chance of bias and so raises the standard of checking required.

check.q: A single new study claims to overturn decades of consistent evidence. What is the most reasonable first reaction?
choices: Accept it because it is the newest
Reject it without reading
Assume the older studies were fraudulent
Treat it as a lead that needs replication before it changes what we know
check.why: Science rests on the weight of many results; one surprising paper is more likely to be an error than a revolution until others reproduce it.

lessons.title: Smoking and Lung Cancer
lessons.mainIdea: Without any experiment on humans, many kinds of evidence together proved that smoking causes lung cancer.
reading: In the first half of the twentieth century, lung cancer went from a rare disease to a common one, and doctors argued about why. Cars, paved roads, factory smoke and cigarettes had all spread at the same time. In 1950 Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill published a *case-control study* from London hospitals: they compared hundreds of patients with lung cancer to similar patients with other diseases and asked about their habits. Almost every lung cancer patient was a smoker, and heavy smokers were far more common among the cases than the controls.

A case-control study looks backward and can be fooled by memory and by how patients are chosen, so Doll and Hill launched a *cohort study* in 1951. They wrote to every doctor in Britain, recorded the smoking habits of about 40,000 who replied, and then simply waited to see who died of what. Within a few years the pattern was unmistakable: the heavier the smoking, the higher the lung cancer death rate, a clear *dose-response* relationship. Doctors who quit saw their risk fall over time. Similar studies in the United States found the same thing.

No one could run a controlled experiment forcing people to smoke, so the case had to be built from the Bradford Hill questions. The association was extremely strong, it showed a dose-response, smoking came before the cancer, it appeared in every country studied, and tar from cigarettes caused tumors when painted on the skin of mice, giving a mechanism. In January 1964 the United States Surgeon General's committee reviewed the evidence and concluded that cigarette smoking causes lung cancer in men.

The tobacco industry responded not by producing better evidence but by manufacturing doubt, funding studies designed to muddy the picture and insisting the question was still open. That strategy is worth remembering, because it has been copied for other products since. The demand for more evidence is a good scientific instinct; the demand for evidence that could never be enough is not.

words.d: a study that compares people who have a condition with similar people who do not, looking backward for differences
a study that records a group's habits or exposures first and then follows them forward to see what happens
a pattern in which more of a suspected cause produces more of the effect

look.title: The 1964 Verdict
look.text: The committee concluded that cigarette smoking is causally related to lung cancer in men, and that the size of its effect far outweighs every other factor examined. The evidence for women, though thinner, pointed the same way. The committee wrote that the risk rises with the number of cigarettes smoked and with the years of smoking, and falls after quitting.
look.cite: Smoking and Health: Report of the Advisory Committee to the Surgeon General of the United States, 1964 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: The committee could not point to a single experiment. Which of the Bradford Hill questions can you find answered in this summary?

check.q: What is the main weakness of a case-control study that led Doll and Hill to start a cohort study?
choices: It looks backward and can be biased by memory and by how patients are selected
It requires too many participants
It cannot include smokers
It takes decades to produce any result
check.why: Case-control studies rely on recalled history and on the choice of cases and controls; a cohort study records exposure first and then watches, avoiding those biases.

check.q: Which finding is an example of dose-response in the doctors study?
choices: Doctors who lived in London had more cancer
Heavier smokers had higher lung cancer death rates than light smokers
All doctors had the same risk
Younger doctors smoked more
check.why: Dose-response means more of the cause produces more of the effect, which is exactly what rising death rates with heavier smoking show.

check.q: How did the tobacco industry respond to the mounting evidence?
choices: It funded studies that proved smoking safe
It immediately accepted the findings
It manufactured doubt by funding studies designed to muddy the picture
It stopped selling cigarettes in 1964
check.why: The industry's strategy was to keep the question looking open, an approach that has been reused for other products since.

lessons.title: The Ozone Layer
lessons.mainIdea: A prediction made from laboratory chemistry was confirmed by measurements a decade later, and the world acted on the evidence.
reading: High in the *stratosphere*, roughly 15 to 35 kilometers up, a thin layer of *ozone*, a molecule of three oxygen atoms, absorbs most of the sun's harmful ultraviolet light. In 1974 the chemists Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland published a warning. *CFCs*, the chlorofluorocarbon gases then used in spray cans, refrigerators and foam, were so stable that nothing at ground level destroyed them. They would drift upward for decades until ultraviolet light broke them apart, releasing chlorine atoms. Each chlorine atom, they calculated, could act as a *catalyst* and destroy thousands of ozone molecules before being removed.

This was a claim built from laboratory rates and a model of the atmosphere, not from any observed loss. Critics, including the companies that made CFCs, said the effect was speculative. Then in 1985 three scientists from the British Antarctic Survey, Joseph Farman, Brian Gardiner and Jonathan Shanklin, reported that the ozone above their Halley Bay station every October had fallen sharply since the 1970s, to far below anything the models had predicted. A satellite had been measuring the same region, but its software had been flagging the extremely low values as instrument errors.

The Antarctic ozone hole was a stronger effect than Molina and Rowland had predicted, and the reason turned out to be ice clouds in the polar winter that speed up the chlorine chemistry. Within two years, in 1987, nations signed the Montreal Protocol to phase out CFCs, and the treaty has been tightened several times since. Molina and Rowland shared the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Paul Crutzen. Measurements show the amount of ozone-destroying chlorine in the stratosphere peaking around the turn of the century and slowly falling, and the ozone layer is now recovering, with the Antarctic hole expected to heal around the 2060s.

The case shows the full arc of an argument from evidence. A mechanism and a prediction came first. Independent measurements confirmed the prediction, and the exceptions, the values too low to believe, turned out to be the most important data. The claim survived attack, the world acted, and later measurements tested whether the action worked.

words.d: the layer of the atmosphere above the weather, roughly 10 to 50 kilometers up, where the ozone layer sits
a molecule of three oxygen atoms that absorbs ultraviolet light high in the atmosphere
chlorofluorocarbon, a stable human-made gas once used in spray cans and refrigerators that releases chlorine high in the atmosphere
a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up, so it can act again and again

look.title: The Numbers Too Low to Believe
look.text: A satellite instrument measures ozone over Antarctica every day. Its software was written to discard any value below a certain floor, on the assumption that such readings must be glitches. For several Octobers it quietly threw away real measurements of the growing ozone hole. Ground scientists with a single old instrument reported the drop first.
look.prompt: Was the decision to flag very low values as errors unreasonable? What should the satellite team have done with flagged data instead of discarding it?

check.q: What was the basis of Molina and Rowland's 1974 warning?
choices: Satellite photographs of the ozone hole
Reports of sunburn in Antarctica
A vote of atmospheric scientists
Laboratory chemistry and a model of how CFCs would break down high in the atmosphere
check.why: Their claim was a prediction from mechanism, not an observation; the observed loss came a decade later.

check.q: Why can a single chlorine atom destroy thousands of ozone molecules?
choices: It acts as a catalyst, speeding the reaction without being used up
Chlorine atoms are very large
Ozone molecules are unstable and explode on contact
Chlorine absorbs ultraviolet light
check.why: A catalyst is regenerated after each reaction cycle, so one chlorine atom can break ozone apart again and again.

check.q: What role did the 1985 Halley Bay measurements play in the argument?
choices: They disproved the CFC theory
They confirmed the predicted ozone loss with independent evidence, and showed it was worse than expected
They showed the ozone hole was natural
They were the first to suggest CFCs might be harmful
check.why: The measurements were the observational test of a prediction made from chemistry, and the size of the loss pushed nations to act.

lessons.title: Vaccines and Autism
lessons.mainIdea: A tiny, flawed study created a fear that enormous, careful studies have repeatedly failed to support.
reading: In February 1998 the medical journal The Lancet published a paper describing twelve children with developmental problems, most of them autism, whose parents linked the symptoms to the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Twelve children, no control group, no comparison to unvaccinated children, and a *hypothesis* raised at a press conference by the lead author, Andrew Wakefield, who suggested the combined vaccine be split up. Vaccination rates in Britain fell. Measles, which had nearly vanished, came back.

The proper way to test the hypothesis is to compare large groups of vaccinated and unvaccinated children and see whether autism is more common in one. Researchers in Denmark, where national health records track every child, did exactly that. A 2002 study of more than 500,000 children found no difference in autism rates. A 2019 study of more than 650,000 children, including children considered at higher risk, found none either. Studies in the United States, Japan and elsewhere agreed. Autism diagnoses have risen, but the rise tracks broader definitions and better screening, and it appears in vaccinated and unvaccinated children alike.

Meanwhile an investigation found that the 1998 paper's data had been altered, that the children had been recruited through lawyers preparing a lawsuit against vaccine makers, and that the lead author had been paid by those lawyers. In 2010 The Lancet *retracted* the paper, and Britain's medical council struck Wakefield from the register of doctors. The paper's central claim had failed every test that evidence can apply: it could not be replicated, its data were unreliable and its author had an undisclosed conflict of interest.

The case matters not because scientists were wrong for a while, which happens, but because of how the two kinds of evidence compare. On one side is a story about twelve children told by a person with a financial stake. On the other are *cohort* studies of more than a million children with no link found. Learning to weigh those two against each other, rather than treating them as two equal sides, is the whole skill this chapter has been about.

words.d: a proposed explanation that can be tested by gathering evidence
formally withdrawn from the scientific record by the journal that published it
a large group of people followed over time to see what happens to them

look.title: Withdrawn From the Record
look.text: In 2010 the editors of The Lancet announced that, following the findings of the medical council's inquiry, it had become clear that several elements of the 1998 paper were incorrect, including statements about how the children were selected and about the approval of the study. The editors said they fully retracted the paper from the published record.
look.cite: Editors of The Lancet, retraction notice for the 1998 paper by Wakefield and others, February 2010 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Retractions are rare and journals dislike issuing them. Why is a system that can retract a paper more trustworthy than one that never does?

check.q: Which weakness of the 1998 paper would a reader of this chapter spot first?
choices: It was written in English
It appeared in a medical journal
It described only twelve children with no control group
It concerned a vaccine
check.why: Twelve cases with no comparison group cannot show whether autism is any more common among vaccinated children than among others.

check.q: What did the large Danish studies find?
choices: That the combined vaccine should be split up
That autism was slightly more common after vaccination
That the results could not be determined
That autism rates were the same in vaccinated and unvaccinated children
check.why: Cohort studies of hundreds of thousands of children found no difference in autism rates, and other countries' studies agreed.

check.q: Why should the 1998 paper and the later cohort studies not be treated as two equal sides of a debate?
choices: One rests on twelve altered cases and a conflict of interest; the others on more than a million children with no link found
Because debates in science are decided by vote
Because the 1998 paper was older and therefore more reliable
Because journals always agree with each other
check.why: Evidence is weighed by its quality and quantity, and the two sides differ enormously in both.

review.q: John Snow's map showed deaths clustered around the Broad Street pump. Why was the brewery evidence so important?
choices: It showed the pump water tasted bad
It was an exception that the miasma theory could not explain but the water theory could
It proved beer cures cholera
It was the only evidence Snow collected
review.why: Brewery workers breathed the same air as their neighbors but drank beer instead of pump water and stayed healthy, which fits the water explanation and not the bad-air one.

review.q: A study finds that students who eat breakfast get higher grades. Which is the best confounding variable to consider?
choices: Breakfast foods contain vitamins
Grades are measured on a 100-point scale
Family income may affect both breakfast habits and school support
Students who eat breakfast wake up earlier
review.why: A hidden factor that drives both breakfast and grades, such as household resources, could create the correlation without breakfast causing better grades.

review.q: Which sample would give the most trustworthy estimate of a city's opinion?
choices: Two million responses to a mailed survey of car owners
The first 500 people who answer an online poll
Ten thousand listeners who call a radio show
One thousand residents chosen at random from all households
review.why: A smaller random sample avoids the systematic bias built into surveys of car owners, volunteers or callers.

review.q: A measurement is reported as 52.3 plus or minus 0.4 grams. A second measurement reads 52.6 plus or minus 0.4 grams. Do they disagree?
choices: No; the difference is smaller than the uncertainties, so they agree
Yes; any difference means one is wrong
Yes; 52.6 is more accurate
Only if a third measurement is taken
review.why: Two results whose uncertainty ranges overlap are consistent with each other; nothing has been detected.

review.q: Why did most laboratories abandon the 1989 cold fusion claim?
choices: The authors withdrew it the next day
They could not replicate the result
It was never peer reviewed
The government banned the research
review.why: Replication by independent labs is the decisive test, and the claim failed it.

review.q: A news story reports that a habit doubles the risk of a rare disease affecting 1 in 10,000 people. What is the absolute risk after doubling?
choices: 1 in 10
About 2 in 10,000
About 1 in 2
review.why: Doubling a relative risk from a baseline of 1 in 10,000 gives about 2 in 10,000, still a very small absolute risk.

review.q: Which piece of evidence gave the smoking and cancer case its mechanism?
choices: The Literary Digest poll
The decline of lung cancer in the 1920s
The Montreal Protocol
Cigarette tar causing tumors when applied to the skin of mice
review.why: Laboratory evidence that a component of smoke causes tumors explained how the association seen in people could be causal.

review.q: What do the ozone and vaccine cases have in common about how evidence was used?
choices: In both, large independent measurements or studies decided the question, not the first claim
In both, a single small study settled the matter
In both, the original claim turned out to be fraudulent
In both, no action was ever taken
review.why: In the ozone case the first claim was confirmed by later data; in the vaccine case the first claim was refuted. Either way the deciding factor was the weight of independent evidence.
